title: Spotify could soon let you host a Jam without Premium
summary: With strings attached, of course.
body: TL;DR Spotify could soon let Free users host their own collaborative Jams, removing the current Premium-only requirement. Jams hosted by Free users may force shuffle, limit skips, and cap the queue for everyone, including Premium participants. App strings in Spotify 9.1.82.19 hint at the change, but there’s no guarantee the feature will actually roll out. Spotify released Jam, a fully collaborative real-time playlist that can be joined by up to 32 individuals, back in September of 2023. It’s one of Spotify’s best features , and it’s turning three next month. To celebrate the occasion, the music streaming giant might finally be ready to make hosting Jams a lot more accessible. For reference, joining and participating in Jams is available to all, but hosting one requires you to be a Spotify Premium subscriber. Essentially, joining someone’s party is a free affair, but if you want to host a party, you’ll have to open up your wallet. That caveat, however, could soon disappear.

title: Android 17 has some new tricks to keep your web traffic private
summary: Here's how Android 17 is locking down your network traffic from prying eyes.
body: TL;DR Google’s implementing a number of new network security upgrades for Android 17. Encrypted Client Hello attempts to solve DNS privacy problems by encrypting server lookups. SMS Blaster protection empowers carriers to block low-security 2G connections by default. Keeping mobile devices secure is one of those jobs that never end, and when it comes to security in Android, Google finds itself constantly working to lock our phones down against external threats. With Android 17 , the company’s already highlighted some of the big ways it’s been improving security , and today Google has a few more updates to share on how your phone is becoming more secure and private that ever. Android 17 makes a number of changes to how devices work with network traffic. One big privacy-protecting one there impacts how apps are able to see your home’s local network, preventing them from probing it for fingerprinting or even spotting vulnerable network hardware. Another we knew about implements Certificate Transparency by default, helping ensure that your phone uses the proper SSL certificates for the server it’s trying to communicate with.
